extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Aristotelian moral philosophy (Nicomachean Ethics)
extracted.subtask_description: Classifying and distinguishing moral character-types in Aristotle's discussion of self-control (Book VII), including criteria based on object-matter, relation to reason, and culpability. Useful for analyzing passages about akrasia, enkrateia, and related states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-Control
rubrics_metrics.description: That Self-Control ... belong[s] to the class of things good and praiseworthy; the man of Self-Control is identical with the man who is apt to abide by his resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterised by refusing, by the influence of reason, to follow the suggestions of lusts; pertains especially to pleasures and pains (bodily appetites). It is contrasted with Imperfect Self-Control and seen as praiseworthy provided it operates via moral choice and reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imperfect Self-Control
rubrics_metrics.description: That the man of Imperfect Self-Control does things at the instigation of his passions, knowing them to be wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often called akrasia. Can be general or limited to particular objects (anger, honour, gain). Its object-matter is primarily bodily pleasures and pains; regarded as blameworthy and in some senses a vice, though distinctions are drawn when the failing is due to disease or the like.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfected Self-Mastery
rubrics_metrics.description: That the man of Perfected Self-Mastery unites the qualities of Self-Control and Endurance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some treat perfect self-mastery as identical with Self-Control. It is the mean state regarding pleasures/pains (especially bodily ones) — the ideal combination of resisting temptation and enduring pain through correct moral choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utter absence of Self-Control
rubrics_metrics.description: He that pursues excessive pleasures and too much avoids things which are painful ... not from moral choice but in spite of his moral choice and intellectual conviction, is termed 'a man utterly void of Self-Control.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marked by incapacity for remorse (hence 'incurable'); acts without moral choice; contrasted with those who fail under strong desire but still possess moral sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Softness
rubrics_metrics.description: Softness is the kindred fault to Endurance in respect of pain: softness = yielding to pains to which most men would be superior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Softness is culpable when it involves choosing to avoid necessary pains; contrasted with Endurance, which is praiseworthy. Part of the scale of characters concerning bodily pains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endurance
rubrics_metrics.description: Endurance is the counterpart of Softness, the ability to withstand pain where most men would yield.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considered praiseworthy if it arises from correct moral choice; part of the virtue spectrum regarding bodily pains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brutishness (brutish states)
rubrics_metrics.description: The brutish man is rare ... found most among barbarians, and some cases of it are caused by disease or maiming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brutish inclinations (e.g., cannibalistic tastes) are not properly called vice; when mastery occurs it is not properly Self-Control in the moral sense because the subject lacks the rational principle. Such states are metaphorically likened to akrasia but are distinct in origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morbid states
rubrics_metrics.description: Some moral states arise from disease or custom and are 'morbid' rather than genuine vices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Morbid inclinations (e.g., pathological fears, compulsions) should be classified differently from moral failures; restraint or yielding in these cases is not the same as moral Self-Control or akrasia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Object-matter: bodily pleasures and pains
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasures and pains which come to a man through Touch and Taste ... constitute the object-matter of the states of utter absence of Self-Control and Perfected Self-Mastery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The central domain for Self-Control, Imperfect Self-Control, Perfected Self-Mastery and utter loss of self-control; distinctions among characters often pivot on whether the object-matter is bodily pleasures/pains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Object-matter: choiceworthy goods (honour, wealth, victory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Things which produce pleasure are either necessary, or objects of choice in themselves ... victor}^, honour, wealth, and such-like good or pleasant things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excess regarding these goods is blameworthy but is typically described as a lack of self-control with a specification (e.g., akrasia in respect of honour or gain) rather than Imperfect Self-Control 'simply'. These cases are analogical, not identical, to akrasia over bodily pleasures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity vs. simplicity of designation
rubrics_metrics.description: Some confound the two characters of the man who has no Self-Control, and the man of Imperfect Self-Control, while others distinguish between them ... men are said to be of Imperfect Self-Control, not simply but with the addition of the thing wherein.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification requires noting whether the failure is 'simply' akrasia (usually bodily pleasures) or akrasia 'in respect of' a particular object (anger, honour, gain); naming reflects this difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge vs Opinion in akrasia
rubrics_metrics.description: That he can so fail when knowing in the strict sense what is right some say is impossible ... they say that it is not Knowledge, but only Opinion, which the man in question has and yet yields to the instigation of his pleasures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle analyses senses of 'knowing' — having knowledge vs exercising it. Failure may occur despite 'knowledge' in a certain sense (e.g., not using knowledge, analogous to being drunk or mad). The distinction affects excusability and classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical Wisdom relation to Imperfect Self-Control
rubrics_metrics.description: It is sometimes said that the man of Practical Wisdom cannot be a man of Imperfect Self-Control, sometimes that men who are Practically Wise and Clever are of Imperfect Self-Control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Debate whether practical wisdom (phronesis) precludes akrasia; Aristotle argues that practical wisdom involves aptitude to act, and so its coexistence with akrasia is problematic though some assert it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of practical syllogism (universal vs particular)
rubrics_metrics.description: All action may be analysed into a syllogism ... one premiss is an universal maxim and the other concerns particulars ... there are two kinds of propositions affecting action, universal and particular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure of Self-Control can be analysed as using the universal but failing to apply/recognise the particular (the minor premise) in action; passions may interfere with the particular premiss that determines moral action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passions as altering cognition (analogy to sleep/drunkenness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Men under the actual operation of passion are in exactly similar conditions [to being asleep, mad, or drunk] ... passions manifestly make changes even in the body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When passions operate, a person may 'know' maxims yet not exercise knowledge; this explains how one may speak moral sayings yet not act on them. Physiological/psychological conditions are relevant to moral responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excusability vs Blame depending on strength of conviction
rubrics_metrics.description: If the opposing conception be not strong but only mild (as in the case of real doubt), the not abiding by it in the face of strong lusts would be excusable: but wickedness is not excusable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a failing is excused depends on whether the agent's conviction was merely opinion/doubt rather than firm knowledge; degrees of belief matter to moral assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insidiousness and naturalness as weighing disgrace
rubrics_metrics.description: Imperfect Self-Control in respect of Lusts is more disgraceful than that in respect of Anger ... Anger in a way listens to Reason but mishears it; Lust ... does not and is therefore more disgraceful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Akrasia regarding lusts is worse because lust is more insidious, less aligned with reason, and often involves pleasure without pain; anger may follow reason more openly and be more excusable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree and scope as moral differentiators
rubrics_metrics.description: A man may be so disposed as to yield to temptations to which most men would be superior, or to be superior to those to which most men would yield ... the moral state of most men is something between the two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral assessment depends on where an individual's dispositions lie relative to the common standard (most men). Characters are graded by degree (leaning to worse or better) rather than binary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remorse as marker of curability and moral status
rubrics_metrics.description: He that has not remorse is incurable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of remorse indicates a deeper moral defect (utter lack of self-control) and makes reform unlikely; remorse is a diagnostic criterion for severity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between vice and analogous failings
rubrics_metrics.description: Wherever nature is really the cause no one would think of calling men of Imperfect Self-Control ... nor ... such as are in a diseased state through custom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the inclination arises from nature or disease, the resulting behaviour is not properly called Vice; classification must separate genuine moral vice from metaphorical resemblances (brutish, morbid).
